title: Read the energy diagram
asks: Several reaction-coordinate diagrams are drawn. Pick the one that fits the reaction described.

know.h: A reaction-coordinate diagram plots energy (up) against the progress of the reaction (left to right): starting materials on the left, products on the right.
Every peak is a transition state. Every valley between two peaks is an intermediate. The number of steps equals the number of peaks, and the number of intermediates is one fewer.
{{Ea}} of a step is the height from the level just before the step up to its peak. For the first step that is from the starting materials. For a later step it is from the intermediate in front of it.
{{dH}} is the products' level minus the starting materials' level. Products lower: exothermic (negative). Products higher: endothermic (positive). The peaks do not enter into it.
The rate-determining step (rds) is the one whose transition state is the highest point of the whole diagram.
Concerted reactions have one hump. {{SN2}}: one hump from start to product, no intermediate. {{E2}}: one hump as well.
{{SN1}} has a valley for the carbocation. The first hump (ionization, ts1) is the highest point and is the rds. The second hump (attack of the nucleophile) is lower.

Drawn in full for tert-butyl bromide and water, {{SN1}} has three steps: ionization, attack of water to give the protonated alcohol, and loss of {{H+}} to a second water. That is three peaks and two valleys (the carbocation and the protonated alcohol).
{{E1}} shares the first step and the carbocation with {{SN1}}. Its second step is removal of a hydrogen next to the cationic carbon: two humps, the first one higher.
The exam question: an exothermic {{SN1}} is the diagram with two humps, a valley between them, the first hump higher, and the products below the starting materials.
Rate comes from {{Ea}}, not from {{dH}}. A very exothermic reaction can still be slow if its barrier is high.

The rate law tells you the shape. If the nucleophile's concentration is in the rate law, it is in the rate-determining transition state: one hump ({{SN2}}, {{E2}}). If only the substrate is in the rate law, the slow step is ionization: two or more humps ({{SN1}}, {{E1}}).
know.from: Lecture 11/03, p. 3; Lecture 11/10, p. 1; Lecture 11/12, p. 1

know.h: For the reverse reaction, read the same diagram from right to left: its {{Ea}} is the height from the products up to the peak.

method: Count the humps: one means concerted (SN2 or E2), two or more means there are intermediates (SN1 or E1).
Mark each valley between humps as an intermediate and name it (for SN1 and E1, the carbocation).
Find the highest peak: the step that climbs to it is the rate-determining step.
Compare the right-hand end with the left-hand end: lower is exothermic, higher is endothermic.
For a number, subtract levels: Ea is peak minus the level before that step, and ΔH is products minus starting materials.
Check every word of the question (exothermic, SN1, rate-determining) against the diagram you picked.

pitfalls.h: Calling a peak an intermediate. Intermediates are valleys. Peaks are transition states.
Reading exothermic or endothermic from the height of a hump instead of from the two ends.
Choosing a two-hump diagram for {{SN1}} without checking that the first hump is the higher one.
Measuring {{Ea}} of a later step from the starting materials instead of from the intermediate before it.
Deciding which reaction is faster from {{dH}}. The barrier decides.
Stopping at the right shape and missing one word of the question, such as exothermic.
